_comment: Per-chart narratives. CI (build_prompt.py -> GitHub Models -> write_narrative.py) overwrites these from live numbers; this committed copy is the fallback so the page always reads well. source = 'fallback' | 'github-models'.

notes.fossil: As of June 2026, WTI crude trades at approximately $84.38 per barrel, Brent crude at $86.99 per barrel, and US regular gasoline at $4.00 per gallon, while Henry Hub natural gas is priced at $2.80 per MMBtu. Indexed to 2019 levels (set at 100), natural gas has shown the greatest volatility among these fuels, peaking sharply in 2022 before retreating, whereas crude oil and gasoline prices have generally moved more in tandem. This volatility in natural gas may be attributed to market and geopolitical factors affecting supply and demand within a tighter and more regionally constrained market. The relative stability of crude and gasoline contrasts with the more erratic natural gas trajectory over recent years.
notes.transition: The levelised cost of electricity, which represents the average cost per megawatt-hour (MWh) of building and operating power-generating assets over their lifetimes, shows significant variation across technologies. Solar photovoltaic (PV) and onshore wind power have levelised costs of $44/MWh and $33/MWh respectively, substantially undercutting new coal at $110/MWh and gas combined cycle gas turbines (CCGT) at $76/MWh. Offshore wind stands at $75/MWh, close to gas costs. Solar PV's cost decline of around 90% since 2010—dropping from approximately $460/MWh to $44/MWh—highlights dramatic technological improvements and cost efficiencies, reshaping the economics of new electricity generation capacity.
notes.currency: An estimated 20% and growing share of global oil trade is now settled outside the US dollar, illustrating a gradual drift from traditional dollar dominance. This estimate is not official but reflects shifts in geopolitical dynamics, notably Russia's pivot towards Asian markets and deals settled in alternative currencies such as the Chinese yuan and Indian rupee. Despite this trend, the US dollar remains the predominant currency in global oil transactions, underscoring its entrenched role in commodity trading. The developments signify evolving but still incremental changes in oil trade currency composition.
notes.now: Current energy markets reveal a complex interplay: fossil fuel prices display varied volatility with natural gas notably more erratic, while renewable electricity costs continue to decline, rendering solar PV and onshore wind more cost-effective than traditional fossil-based generation. Simultaneously, the currency composition of global oil trade reflects subtle shifts, with rising non-dollar settlements driven by geopolitical realignments. Together, these factors paint a nuanced picture of the evolving energy landscape as of mid-2026.
